extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of Plato; philosophers and educators interested in the role of poetry in moral education
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts Plato's standards for admitting, judging, or using poetry and imitative arts in education and civic life (from the Republic excerpt). Focuses on how poetry relates to truth, the soul, and civic virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry as imitation (thrice removed from truth)
rubrics_metrics.description: The imitator has no knowledge worth mentioning of what he imitates; imitation is only a kind of play or sport and is concerned with that which is thrice removed from the truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato's analogy: a painter makes a likeness of a cobbler without understanding cobbling; the poet 'lays on the colours of the several arts' but understands them only enough to imitate. Therefore poetic representations are likenesses of appearances, not of true forms, and cannot be relied upon for genuine knowledge or instruction in virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creator must possess practical/authoritative knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: The one who uses (practitioner) has the greatest experience and knows the right form; the maker (imitator) attains only to correct belief from the user and not true knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the horseman knows the right bit and reins, the painter does not. Thus an artist who lacks practical authority over the subject should not be taken as an expert on its goodness or function; authenticity of knowledge is required when art claims to represent or teach a craft or virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect on the soul: poetry addresses inferior (irrational) parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry and imitative art are concerned with an inferior part of the soul; they awaken and nourish feelings and impair the reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because imitative arts stimulate the non-rational elements (passions, emotions) rather than the rational/calculating principle, they risk strengthening irrational impulses and weakening the soul's proper ordering. Works that primarily appeal to reason are preferable for education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral impact: poetry stirs passions that undermine virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry feeds and waters the passions — pity, laughter, lust, anger, desire, pain, pleasure — instead of drying them up; it lets them rule when they ought to be controlled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: enjoying another's drawn-out lament in recitation while condemning such behavior in oneself; laughing at indecent jokes on stage but avoiding them in private. Because poetry satisfies and strengthens these instincts, it can make people act in ways they'd otherwise restrain, thereby corrupting character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form (melody/rhythm) can seduce despite ignorance
rubrics_metrics.description: Melody and rhythm have a sweet influence by nature that causes listeners to think a poet speaks well even when he understands nothing of the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato notes that tales 'make a poor appearance when stripped of the colours which music puts upon them, and recited in simple prose.' Evaluators should be wary of being persuaded by musical form or eloquence alone; test content by considering it without musical/ornamental effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educational suitability: poetry must promote law, reason and virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry should be admitted only if it serves the law and the reason of mankind; otherwise, pleasure and pain will be the rulers in the State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In a well-ordered polity, works used in education must foster the rational principle, temperance, and justice. Any art that encourages the domination of pleasure/pain over reason is disqualifying for public education and civic formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible subject-matter (content restriction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Only hymns to the gods and praises of famous men are the only poetry which ought to be admitted into the State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato draws a hard content boundary: epic, lyric, or 'honeyed' poetry that portrays human passions and ambiguous moral examples should be excluded unless it demonstrably advances virtue and the common good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Popularity vs truth: beware art made to please the masses
rubrics_metrics.description: The imitative poet who aims at being popular will prefer the passionate and fitful temper which is easily imitated, rather than addressing the rational principle of the soul.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Popularity-seeking artists tend to cultivate easily imitable emotions and spectacle. When evaluating creative work, give lower weight to works that primarily aim for popular emotional effect rather than truth, moral instruction, or rational uplift.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditional admission: poetry must prove usefulness to State and life
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry may be allowed to return from exile only if it can 'prove her title to exist in a well-ordered State' by showing not only that she is pleasant but also useful to States and to human life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato proposes a procedural test: require defenders of poetry to make a case (in metre or prose) that their art has civic and moral utility. If they cannot, the art should be excluded despite its charms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid representing or praising behaviors one would condemn in oneself
rubrics_metrics.description: It is inconsistent to admire in dramatic representation what one would abominate or be ashamed of in one's own person (e.g., excessive lamentation, shameless jests).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluators should note the moral inconsistency of works that elicit approval when depicting vice or cowardice in others but teach contempt for such behavior in real life. Works that train sympathy for vice or for unmanly behavior are harmful to moral formation and should be rejected.
